title: Utilitarianism: Bentham and Mill
welcome_lead: Enter the workshop of nineteenth-century reform where Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill argued that the good is the greatest happiness of the greatest number.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on classical utilitarianism, the hedonic calculus, Mill's qualitative pleasures, and act versus rule utilitarianism.
final_note: You have followed the consequentialist thread from Bentham's calculus to Mill's higher pleasures.

walkthroughs.body_html: In An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), Bentham declares that 'nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure'. The hedonic calculus weighs intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (nearness), fecundity (likelihood of more pleasure), purity (freedom from pain) and extent (number of persons affected). This is a strictly quantitative hedonism.

Mill, in Utilitarianism (1863), insisted that pleasures differ in quality, not just quantity. 'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.' Competent judges who have experienced both will prefer the higher pleasure, which gives Mill a way to dodge the 'doctrine worthy only of swine' objection.

Act utilitarianism risks justifying horrors (the sheriff who hangs an innocent man to prevent a riot). Rule utilitarianism replies that a rule against punishing the innocent yields more utility long-term. Critics like Bernard Williams argue rule utilitarianism collapses into act utilitarianism whenever breaking the rule would maximise utility (the 'rule worship' charge).

options: Intensity
Duration
Nobility
Extent

mcqs.q: Mill's distinction between higher and lower pleasures is:
options: Quantitative
Qualitative
Based on duration alone
Identical to Bentham's view

mcqs.q: What does utilitarianism say is right action?
options: Act utilitarianism is about action movies and rule utilitarianism is about laws.
The action that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number — judged by consequences, not intentions or rules.
Whatever makes you personally happy is the right thing to do.
Utilitarianism says you should always tell the truth.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between act and rule utilitarianism?
options: Act utilitarianism judges each individual action by its consequences; rule utilitarianism follows rules that, if generally adopted, would produce the most good — sacrificing case-by-case calculation for predictability and fairness.
Act and rule utilitarianism are basically the same approach.
Act utilitarianism is about action movies and rule utilitarianism is about laws.
Do whatever your conscience tells you to do.

mcqs.q: What does Kant's categorical imperative require?
options: Do whatever your conscience tells you to do.
Acting only on maxims you could will to be universal laws, and treating people as ends in themselves, never merely as means.
Utilitarianism says you should always tell the truth.
Treat others how you would like to be treated.
